subject: AI & Agents
title: AI Training Is Not Programming
description: A micro-lesson that makes AI Training Is Not Programming usable.

hook.text: Nobody sat down and wrote 'if user asks X, respond Y' for ChatGPT. It wasn't programmed that way.

buildup.text: Traditional software follows explicit rules written by programmers for every situation.

discovery.text: Modern AI learns behavior from data. The programmer designs the architecture; the data shapes the behavior.

twist.text: This means even the creators often can't explain why their AI makes specific decisions.

climax.text: It's more like gardening than engineering — you create conditions for growth, not the growth itself.

punchline.text: We didn't write the AI's mind. We grew it.

quiz.question: How does AI training differ from traditional programming?
options: AI learns behavior from data rather than following explicit rules
AI and traditional programming are the same process
AI requires manual rules for every possible input

details.summary: Training an AI model is fundamentally different from traditional programming. Programmers write explicit rules; AI trainers provide examples and let the model discover patterns on its own.
details.whyItMatters: Conflating training with programming creates confusion about how AI systems work and how they fail. Understanding the difference clarifies why AI behavior can be unpredictable.
takeaways: Traditional programming writes explicit step-by-step rules
AI training lets models learn patterns from example data
Learned behavior can be unpredictable unlike coded instructions

faq.question: What is the key difference between training and programming?
faq.answer: Programming specifies exact instructions for every scenario. Training shows the model thousands of examples and lets it infer patterns. The developer controls the process but not the exact learned rules.

faq.question: Why does the training versus programming distinction matter?
faq.answer: It explains why AI can fail unexpectedly. Programmed systems fail in predictable ways. Trained systems can produce surprising errors because their learned rules are opaque and emergent.
